difficultyReason: The stimulus weaves three errors together: equivocation on 'natural' (uncultivated vs. chemical-free), a universal generalization from a non-representative sample of heirloom tomatoes, and a sufficient-for-necessary swap turning 'naturalness suffices for nutritional value' into 'natural crops are the only nutritious crops.' The correct answer replicates all three moves.
stimulus: Heirloom tomatoes grown in the wild woods near Asheville contain none of the synthetic pesticides applied on industrial farms, so they are entirely natural. And since everything natural is nutritionally superior, we may conclude that only wild-grown heirloom tomatoes are nutritionally superior to their cultivated counterparts.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Old-growth cedar harvested from the remote Alaskan coast has no artificial preservatives, and so it is entirely pure. Since everything pure is structurally stronger than its alternatives, we may conclude that only coastal old-growth cedar is structurally stronger than kiln-dried pine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the vineyards of the Mosel Valley use no herbicides, their Rieslings contain no residues. Rieslings with no residues are widely preferred by sommeliers, so Mosel Rieslings are widely preferred by sommeliers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raw honey from alpine meadows contains no added sugars. Therefore, since consumers prefer foods with no added sugars, consumers prefer raw alpine honey to processed honey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Handwoven rugs from rural Anatolia use no synthetic dyes, so they are entirely authentic. Because authentic rugs appreciate in value, handwoven Anatolian rugs appreciate in value more than machine-made rugs do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wild salmon caught off the Kenai Peninsula are free of farm-pen antibiotics, and so they are purer than farmed salmon. Since purer fish are healthier, wild Kenai salmon are healthier than farmed salmon.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: it equivocates on 'pure' (free of preservatives vs. unadulterated in any sense), generalizes from a narrow example to a universal 'everything pure is stronger,' and flips a sufficient condition ('purity suffices for strength') into a necessary one ('only this cedar is stronger'). The compound flaw is identical in structure to the stimulus.
explanations.B: Contains a linking chain but no equivocation and no sufficient/necessary reversal — the conclusion follows validly from the premises as stated.
explanations.C: A single correlation-to-preference step; no universal claim and no 'only' reversal in the conclusion.
explanations.D: Equivocates on 'authentic' but concludes with a comparative claim, not an 'only' exclusivity claim; it is missing the sufficient/necessary flip.
explanations.E: Valid chain: free of antibiotics → purer → healthier. No equivocation, no universal overreach, no exclusivity reversal.

difficultyReason: Three compounding errors: (1) composition fallacy (what is true of a part of the orchestra is ascribed to the whole); (2) ambiguity on 'balanced' (acoustic balance vs. repertoire balance); (3) the conclusion then inverts the conditional, treating 'balance implies acclaim' as 'only balanced orchestras are acclaimed.' Each answer choice replicates some but not all of these moves.
stimulus: Every section of the Prague Chamber Orchestra — strings, winds, brass — produces a balanced sound on its own. So the orchestra as a whole must be balanced. Because only balanced orchestras win international acclaim, the Prague Chamber Orchestra must be among the acclaimed ensembles of its generation.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each of the attorneys at Merton & Voss is persuasive in oral argument, so Merton & Voss is a persuasive firm. Because persuasive firms win most of their trials, Merton & Voss wins most of its trials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every department at Halloran College — humanities, sciences, arts — is rigorous on its own. So the college as a whole is rigorous. And because only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars, Halloran must be among the colleges producing Rhodes Scholars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each player on the Winfield hockey team has excellent stickhandling, so the team must have excellent stickhandling. Teams with excellent stickhandling tend to win championships, so Winfield will probably win the championship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every chapter in Professor Lin's new book is clearly written, so her book is clearly written. Clearly written books sell well, so her book will sell well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each division of Volterra Motors meets its quarterly targets, so Volterra meets its annual targets. Since companies that meet annual targets are admired by investors, Volterra is admired by investors.

explanations.correct: B replicates all three moves: composition (each department rigorous → college rigorous); equivocation on 'rigorous' (department-level rigor vs. institutional reputation); and the 'only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars' conditional flipped into a claim that Halloran is among the Rhodes-producing colleges. The compound flaw matches precisely.
explanations.A: Composition is present, but there is no 'only' conditional reversal; the chain is linear.
explanations.C: Hedged conclusion ('probably') and no equivocation on 'stickhandling'; missing two of the three moves.
explanations.D: Simple composition followed by a valid inference; no ambiguity and no reversal.
explanations.E: Contains a different compositional flaw (quarterly vs. annual) and a scope shift, but no sufficient/necessary reversal in the final step.

difficultyReason: Three stacked errors: (1) correlation mistaken for causation between statin use and reduced cardiac events; (2) the causal claim is then universalized beyond the study population; (3) base-rate reversal — because most patients with low cardiac events are on statins, a patient on statins is presumed to have low cardiac event risk. The correct answer must stack all three.
stimulus: A ten-year observational study in Uppsala found that patients taking statins had 30% fewer cardiac events than those not taking them. It follows that statins prevent cardiac events in any patient population. Since most low-risk cardiac patients in our clinic are on statins, any patient we place on statins will likely be a low-risk cardiac patient.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longitudinal survey in Oslo showed that readers of literary fiction score higher on empathy tests than non-readers. Therefore, literary fiction cultivates empathy in any reader. Because most empathic professionals read literary fiction, any professional who begins reading literary fiction will likely become empathic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A city-wide study found that neighborhoods with more trees have lower asthma rates. So trees must improve respiratory health. Therefore, planting trees in any city will reduce its asthma rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys show that frequent meditators report lower stress. Since meditation calms the mind, anyone who meditates will feel less stressed. Most people who feel less stressed have stable relationships, so meditation stabilizes relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regional audit found that firms using agile methodology deliver software faster than those using waterfall. Agile therefore accelerates delivery universally. Anyone who adopts agile will deliver software faster than their waterfall competitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A decade-long trial showed that communities consuming more olive oil had lower rates of stroke. So olive oil prevents stroke. Since most stroke-free communities consume olive oil, any community that begins consuming olive oil will be stroke-free.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: (1) correlation-to-causation (readers scoring higher → fiction cultivates empathy); (2) universal overreach ('in any reader'); (3) base-rate reversal — 'most empathic professionals read fiction, so any professional who reads will be empathic.' The compound is exact.
explanations.B: Correlation-to-causation plus universalization, but no base-rate reversal — the final step is a straightforward (if unwarranted) generalization.
explanations.C: Introduces a second causal chain (meditation → relationships) rather than a base-rate inversion; the flaw pattern diverges on the third step.
explanations.D: Two moves only — correlation-to-causation and universalization. Missing the base-rate reversal step.
explanations.E: Close, but the conclusion is 'stroke-free,' a certainty claim, while the stimulus concludes a probabilistic 'likely be low-risk.' The strength mismatch makes E off-by-one.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) ad hominem dismissal that slides into (2) a genetic fallacy generalized into a universal claim about a field, which in turn (3) inverts a conditional — from 'biased sources cannot establish truth' to 'only unbiased sources can.' The correct answer must replicate the slide from personal attack through field-level generalization to necessary-condition inversion.
stimulus: The historian Ackroyd was a lifelong royalist, so his account of the Glorious Revolution cannot be trusted. Indeed, because any historian with political loyalties is biased, the entire field of political history is compromised. It follows that only accounts by politically unaffiliated historians can give us genuine historical knowledge.
questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The critic Beaumont was a declared modernist, so his review of the new opera is biased. Because biased critics misjudge opera, Beaumont misjudged this opera, and so his review should be disregarded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The economist Halvarsson advised a sitting government, so her forecasts cannot be trusted. Since any economist advising a government is compromised, the entire discipline of macroeconomic forecasting is unreliable. Therefore, only forecasts produced by economists with no governmental ties can qualify as legitimate forecasts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The journalist Ruiz has taken corporate sponsorship, so his coverage of that corporation should be discounted. Sponsored journalism is often biased, and biased journalism misleads readers. Therefore, Ruiz's readers are likely misled about the corporation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Pelham once consulted for an industrial client, and so his published findings are suspect. Because published findings by consultants are frequently disputed, Dr. Pelham's findings will probably be disputed as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The statistician Okoro worked briefly for a polling firm, so she is biased. Since bias invalidates polling, her polls are invalid. The only valid polls are those she did not design.

explanations.correct: B mirrors the slide: personal attack on Halvarsson → universal claim about all economists with government ties → field-wide compromise → only unaffiliated economists produce 'legitimate' forecasts. All three moves match the stimulus structure.
explanations.A: Personal attack plus a chain, but no field-level generalization and no inversion to 'only X can produce knowledge.'
explanations.C: Hedged throughout ('often,' 'likely') and stops at a reader-level conclusion; no 'only' reversal.
explanations.D: Two moves, not three — no field-wide claim.
explanations.E: Personal attack and 'only' reversal, but the scope is restricted to Okoro's own polls rather than being universalized across a field.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) hasty generalization from one startup to all startups; (2) equivocation on 'fail' (bankruptcy vs. failing to reach projections); (3) denying the antecedent — from 'poor management leads to failure' to 'without poor management, no failure.' The correct answer must compound all three.
stimulus: Morrow Analytics missed its revenue projections last quarter and was labeled a failure. It follows that every startup that misses projections has failed. And since poor management is what causes startups to fail, any startup with competent management will meet its projections.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments displays a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Riverton public library closed after its budget was cut, which proves that budget cuts destroy libraries. Every library facing budget cuts is at risk of being destroyed, and since inadequate public support causes library destruction, libraries with adequate public support are safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kessler Foods recalled a batch of soup contaminated with listeria, which shows it cut corners on inspection. Therefore, every food manufacturer that recalls a batch has cut corners on inspection. Because corner-cutting causes recalls, any manufacturer that does not cut corners will never issue a recall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The manuscript Vellum & Ink was rejected by its publisher, so it was deemed unpublishable. Every manuscript rejected by a publisher is unpublishable, and since a weak premise causes rejection, manuscripts without weak premises are never rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Santillan's clinic was cited by the regulator last year, meaning her clinic was compromised. Every clinic cited by regulators is compromised, and because lax protocols cause citations, any clinic with strict protocols will never be cited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The engineering firm Aldebaran lost its bid on the bridge contract, so it is uncompetitive. Since every firm that loses a major bid is uncompetitive, and uncompetitive firms have poor leadership, Aldebaran's leadership is poor.

explanations.correct: B compounds the same three moves: hasty generalization (Kessler's recall → every recall means cut corners); equivocation on 'recall' (one batch vs. manufacturer reputation); and denying the antecedent (corner-cutting causes recalls → no corner-cutting, no recalls). The strength of the conclusion ('never') matches the stimulus's universal closure.
explanations.A: Generalization and denial-of-antecedent are present, but 'destroy' and 'at risk of being destroyed' are not equivocal — the argument holds 'destruction' constant. Two of three moves.
explanations.C: Close, but the final step shifts the dimension: 'weak premise causes rejection' is inverted, but without the equivocation on 'rejected' vs. 'unpublishable' being fully carried through.
explanations.D: The conclusion retains the same term ('cited') throughout — no equivocation. And the final 'never' is a denial of antecedent, but only two of three moves.
explanations.E: Runs the chain forward rather than inverting the final conditional; the structure is linear rather than compound-flawed in the stimulus's way.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) percentage-vs-absolute confusion (share of workforce vs. head count); (2) universalization across a region; (3) affirming the consequent — from 'automation reduces manufacturing share' to 'because manufacturing share has declined, automation must have caused it.' The correct answer must stack all three.
stimulus: In the Ruhr region, manufacturing has fallen from 40% of the workforce to 25% over two decades, meaning fewer people than ever work in manufacturing there. This pattern must therefore hold across all industrialized regions. And since automation reduces manufacturing's share of the workforce, the decline in the Ruhr must have been caused by automation.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Kyoto, tourism has fallen from 30% of service-sector employment to 15% over a decade, so fewer residents than ever work in tourism there. The same must be true of all historic cities in Asia. And because budget airlines draw tourism away from traditional hubs, Kyoto's decline must have been caused by budget airlines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In several European capitals, the share of cycling commuters has risen above 20%. This trend holds across all urban centers. Because bike lanes increase cycling share, the rise in these capitals must have been caused by bike lane construction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Across the Midwest, family farms now account for 10% of agricultural output, down from 25% thirty years ago. This must be true nationwide. Consolidation reduces the family farm share, and so consolidation caused the decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In Lombardy, the textile industry's workforce share dropped from 35% to 20%, which means fewer workers than ever are in textiles. This pattern extends across all Mediterranean economies. Since offshoring reduces textile employment share, offshoring must explain the Lombardy decline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coal mining in Appalachia fell from 18% of regional employment to 6%, so coal employs fewer people than ever in the region. The same must be true in every coal-producing country. And because environmental regulation reduces coal's share of employment, regulation caused the Appalachian decline.

explanations.correct: D mirrors all three moves precisely: percentage-to-absolute confusion ('35% to 20%' → 'fewer workers than ever'); universalization ('all Mediterranean economies'); and affirming the consequent (offshoring reduces textile share; share fell; therefore offshoring caused it). The compound matches the stimulus closely, and the domain is economics — distinct from the stimulus's industrial context but structurally identical.
explanations.A: Present all three moves but the causal agent named ('budget airlines') and the quantity ('service-sector employment') introduce a scope mismatch — the stimulus's causal agent is more tightly tied to the dependent variable than A's is.
explanations.B: Missing the percentage-to-absolute confusion — the rise in cycling share is stated as a share, not translated into absolute counts.
explanations.C: Lacks the 'fewer than ever' absolute-number mistranslation; the argument stays in percentage terms. Two of three moves.
explanations.E: Close, but 'fewer people than ever' is a stronger absolute claim and the scope ('every coal-producing country') is broader than the stimulus's 'all industrialized regions' — off-by-one in breadth.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) false dichotomy (either strict liability or no accountability); (2) this dichotomy is supported by an equivocation on 'accountability' (legal liability vs. moral responsibility); (3) the necessary condition is then flipped into a sufficient one. The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
stimulus: Either manufacturers are held strictly liable for defective products, or there is no product accountability at all. Strict liability is therefore the only way to ensure accountability. And since accountability is necessary for consumer trust, imposing strict liability will by itself be enough to restore consumer trust in our markets.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either a university enforces a strict plagiarism policy, or it has no academic integrity. A strict policy is thus the only route to integrity. And because integrity is necessary for scholarly reputation, a strict plagiarism policy by itself will restore the university's scholarly reputation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either a newspaper has a strong editorial board, or it has no standards at all. Therefore, a strong editorial board is the only way to maintain standards. Because standards are important to readers, a strong editorial board will make readers loyal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A museum either charges admission or it cannot maintain its collection. Charging admission is thus the only viable model. Since funds are necessary for maintenance, charging admission will be sufficient for maintenance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a city has strong zoning or it has chaotic development. Zoning is the only cure for chaotic development. And because orderly development is desirable, zoning will make the city's development orderly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either athletes are subject to random drug testing, or doping goes unchecked. Random testing is thus the only remedy. Because unchecked doping harms the sport's credibility, random testing will by itself restore the sport's credibility.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: false dichotomy (strict policy vs. no integrity); equivocation on 'integrity' (policy enforcement vs. scholarly integrity); and the necessary-to-sufficient flip (integrity necessary for reputation → strict policy sufficient for reputation). The domain shift to academia leaves the structure intact.
explanations.B: False dichotomy and a chain, but the final inference is a reasonable probabilistic claim — no necessary-to-sufficient inversion of the right shape.
explanations.C: Explicitly labels the necessary-to-sufficient move, but lacks the equivocation step that makes the stimulus a three-error compound.
explanations.D: All three moves are present in broad outline but the equivocation on 'orderly' vs. 'zoning' is thin; the argument reads more like a two-step chain.
explanations.E: Very close, but shares a domain with the stimulus (legal/regulatory accountability) and keeps the word 'credibility' stable throughout — no equivocation. Two of three moves.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to authority by a non-expert (a successful poet pronouncing on neuroscience); (2) that authority claim is then generalized across a whole field; (3) circular reasoning — the conclusion ('creativity requires solitude') is smuggled in as a premise ('creative work only happens alone'). The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
stimulus: The celebrated poet Vernier has said that he composes only in solitude, so all neuroscience of creativity must treat solitude as essential. Indeed, creative work — being work that can only happen alone — requires solitude; and since what requires solitude cannot flourish in collaborative settings, genuine creativity cannot flourish in collaborative settings.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The renowned chef Kilbane insists that great cuisine demands only the freshest local produce, so all food science must treat freshness as the decisive variable. Great cuisine — being cuisine that only local produce can produce — requires local produce; and since what requires local produce cannot come from long supply chains, genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The celebrated architect Nesbitt has said that great buildings require symmetry, so architectural theory must prioritize symmetry. Symmetrical buildings tend to last longer than asymmetrical ones, so the best-lasting buildings are symmetrical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The acclaimed composer Viana claims that rhythm is the heart of music, so music theorists must agree. Since rhythm is the heart of music, a piece without rhythm is not music. Therefore a piece without rhythm cannot be called music.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The renowned physicist Hertzen has argued that quantum effects dominate at small scales, so quantum theory should focus there. Because quantum effects dominate at small scales, and what dominates at small scales must be studied there, quantum theory belongs at small scales.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The celebrated novelist Orellana has written that novels must have strong characters, so critics should weight characterization highly. Since strong characters require depth, and depth comes from solitude, novelists must work alone.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: non-expert authority (a chef on food science); field-wide generalization ('all food science must treat freshness as decisive'); and circular reasoning ('cuisine that only local produce can produce' smuggled in to conclude 'genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains'). The compound is identical.
explanations.B: Authority plus a causal chain, but no circularity — the conclusion 'best-lasting buildings are symmetrical' is independent of the premises.
explanations.C: Contains circularity but lacks the field-wide generalization step; the argument stays narrow.
explanations.D: The conclusion is a tautological restatement of the premise rather than a smuggled-in circular claim; the structure is flatter than the stimulus.
explanations.E: Authority and a chain, but the final inference borrows the stimulus's own vocabulary ('solitude') without replicating its three-step compound flaw.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to tradition; (2) a slippery-slope inference from one regulatory change to civilizational decline; (3) conflation of 'legal permission' with 'moral endorsement.' The correct answer must match all three.
stimulus: For centuries, common law has treated inherited property as a fundamental right, and so it must remain so. Any reform that narrows inheritance will inevitably unravel the entire edifice of private property. Because the law permits inheriting property, the state clearly endorses the moral goodness of transferring wealth across generations, and any challenge to that endorsement is a challenge to civilization itself.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For decades, our municipal code has permitted single-family zoning, and so it must remain so. Any reform that allows multifamily housing will inevitably unravel the entire neighborhood character. Because zoning permits single-family homes, the city endorses the moral goodness of that way of life, and any challenge to it is a challenge to community itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For generations, our university has required a Latin examination for all graduates, and so the requirement should remain. Removing Latin will weaken classical education. Because the university tests Latin, it values classical learning, and challenging the test is challenging classical learning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Our courts have long allowed juries to decide capital cases, so they must continue to do so. Removing the jury will undermine confidence in the legal system, and because juries are used, the legal system clearly endorses lay decision-making.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The constitution permits free assembly, so free assembly must be preserved. Restricting assembly would unravel democratic culture. Since the constitution permits assembly, the state approves of assembly, and assembling is therefore a civic virtue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For a century the tax code has exempted certain charitable gifts, and so this exemption must persist. Narrowing it will slowly erode all philanthropy, and because the code permits the exemption, the government formally approves of charitable giving.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: appeal to tradition (decades of single-family zoning); slippery slope (any reform unravels neighborhood character); conflation of legal permission with moral endorsement ('the city endorses the moral goodness' of single-family living). Closes with the civilizational-stakes rhetoric matching the stimulus.
explanations.B: Tradition and a weak consequence claim, but the slope is not 'unraveling' scale and the legal-moral conflation is weakly drawn.
explanations.C: Tradition and conflation present, but no slippery slope — the consequence claim is bounded ('confidence in the legal system').
explanations.D: Conflation and a slope, but the tradition appeal is replaced by a straight appeal to the constitution; the third move is missing its traditional framing.
explanations.E: Tradition and conflation, but the slope is described as 'erode' rather than the stimulus's systemic-unraveling frame, and the civilizational stakes are absent — off-by-one in scope.

difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) survivorship bias (only surviving languages are studied); (2) the resulting pattern is generalized into a universal linguistic claim; (3) the generalization is then used to predict the future — past success becomes a guarantee of continued success. The correct answer must replicate all three.
stimulus: Every surviving European language today has a written tradition going back at least five hundred years, so all European languages have always had long written traditions. Since languages with long written traditions persist, and since written tradition guarantees persistence, Basque — with its long written tradition — is guaranteed to persist for another five centuries.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every established monastery in Ireland has continuously kept a scriptorium for at least eight centuries, so all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria. Since monasteries with scriptoria endure, and because a scriptorium guarantees endurance, Glendalough Monastery — with its eight-century scriptorium — is guaranteed to endure another eight centuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every skyscraper still standing in Chicago was built before 1960, so Chicago skyscrapers have always been built in that era. Because pre-1960 skyscrapers are sturdy, the Monadnock Building, which predates 1960, will continue to stand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every bank that survived the 2008 crisis had diversified holdings, so all banks at that time had diversified holdings. Since diversified banks tend to weather downturns, Commerzbank, which is diversified, will weather any future downturn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All surviving Etruscan bronzes show a high tin content, so Etruscan bronzes uniformly contained high tin. Because high-tin bronzes resist corrosion, the Arezzo Chimera — a high-tin Etruscan bronze — will resist corrosion for centuries to come.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every jazz standard still performed today was composed before 1970, so jazz standards have always dated to that era. Because pre-1970 standards have lasting appeal, 'Mood Indigo' will continue to be performed.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: survivorship bias ('every established monastery' = those that survived); universal generalization ('all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria'); and the leap from 'guarantees endurance' to a future-prediction certainty ('guaranteed to endure another eight centuries'). The compound is identical and the domain shift (language to religious institutions) is clean.
explanations.B: Survivorship and generalization, but the conclusion is softer ('will continue to stand') and lacks the certainty language — off-by-one in strength.
explanations.C: Survivorship and generalization, but the final claim is narrowed ('any future downturn') and depends on a tendency rather than a guarantee — two of three moves.
explanations.D: Survivorship and generalization present, but the conclusion concerns a material property rather than a temporal persistence claim — the domain of the third move doesn't match.
explanations.E: Survivorship and a generalization, but the conclusion 'will continue to be performed' is a tendency-style claim, not a guarantee-level prediction; the third move is weaker than the stimulus's.
